subject: Differences in size-shape plotting & ANOVA vs homogeneity of slopes test, so did the trajectory analysis

messages.author: 0115fa6682bc8072
messages.subject: Differences in size-shape plotting & ANOVA vs homogeneity of slopes test, so did the trajectory analysis
parts:
Dear all,

I am testing the differences in allometry in a test and control group of mice. Each group has two ontogenetic stages: P28 and P60.

1) I ran an ANOVA to test interaction between size & groups first. The results shows an insignificant interaction effect (p-value = 0.258).

> fit_size <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) * groups,  data = gdf_size,
print.progress = FALSE)

                                 Df        SS                 MS              Rsq           F               Z              Pr(>F)    
log(Csize)                1   0.024298    0.0242978    0.35307     9.8733     4.2532      0.001 ***
groups                     1   0.011943     0.0119432    0.17355     4.8531     3.6215      0.001 ***
log(Csize):groups  1   0.003046     0.0030464    0.04427     1.2379     0.6874      0.258    
Residuals                 1. 2 0.029532  0.0024610    0.42912                        
Total                          1. 5 0.068819   

The regScore & Predline plotting also confirm the very similar allometric trajectories in two groups by running (output plot attached):
> plotAllometry(fit_size, size = gdf_size$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "RegScore",
pch = 19, col = as.numeric(interaction(gdf_size$groups)))
> plotAllometry(fit_size, size = gdf_size$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "PredLine",
pch = 19, col = as.numeric(interaction(gdf_size$groups)))

2) However, the test of homogeneity of slopes using 'Pairwise()' shows a large angle of 49 degree between the allometric slopes of two groups, though the p-value 0.077. 

> PW3 <- pairwise(fit_size, groups = as.factor(gdf_size$groups), covariate = log(gdf_size$Csize))
> summary(PW3, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC",
   angle.type = "deg")
Result:
                        r                      angle             UCL (95%)        Z                   Pr > angle
control:test   0.6477955    49.6244          51.05174        1.506624      0.077

Even though the result shows insignificance, but an angle of 49 degree appears to be too large as the RegScore and PredLine plots showed nearly parallel allometric trajectories.

I hope I can directly use 'fit_size', which is 'coords~log(Csize)*Groups'. I assume it would randomize the size*group interaction to test the differences between  size-shape slopes in each group

I then did an additional trajectory analysis since each group has two distinct ontogenetic stages: P28 and P60. Therefore, the linear model includes an interaction of group*stage:

>fit_TA <- procD.lm(coords~groups*stages, data = gdf_size)

You can also see that 'fit_TA' shows an insignificant effect of "group*stage" interaction (p-value = 0.550):
>summary(fit_TA)
                          Df       SS           MS                Rsq           F               Z               Pr(>F)    
groups              1    0.018256   0.0182560   0.26528   5.6613    3.05408     0.001 ***
stages               1   0.009202    0.0092017   0.13371   2.8535    2.46277     0.025 *  
groups:stages  1   0.002665    0.0026647   0.03872  0.8264    -0.13343     0.550    
Residuals          12  0.038696   0.0032247   0.56229                          
Total                 15   0.068819   

>TA <- trajectory.analysis(fit_TA,  groups = gdf_size$groups,  traj.pts = gdf_size$stages, print.progress = FALSE)
>TP <- plot(TA,  pch = as.numeric(as.factor(gdf_size$groups)) + 20, bg = as.numeric(as.factor(gdf_size$stages)),  cex = 0.7,  col = "gray")
>add.trajectories(TP, traj.pch = c(21, 22), start.bg = 1, end.bg = 2)

You can see the attached plot of trajectories showed nearly parallel lines, consistent with Procrustes ANOVA and allometry plotting. 

However, again, the test of angles between two trajectory vectors showed a large angle of 54.1 degree, though the p-value is 0.083.

> summary(TA, attribute = "TC", angle.type = "deg") 

Pairwise correlations between trajectories, plus statistics
                        r                   angle          UCL (95%)      Z                   Pr > angle
control:test  0.5863598   54.10089  57.12142       1.475715      0.083

Could you give me some advice about this sharp differences between angles calculated from test of slopes vs. plotting & ANOVA? Did I construct the linear model run for test of slopes & trajectory angles? Thank you very much!

Chi

messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] Differences in size-shape plotting & ANOVA vs homogeneity of slopes test, so did the trajectory analysis
parts:
Chi,

 

Human intuition fails us on interpreting angles in high-dimensionsal spaces. One cannot interpret an angle of say, 45 degrees and consider it large or small based on what we think in a 2D space.

 

In high-dimensional spaces there are many, many directions that confer such an angle, which may explain why it is not surprising (ie not significant) in your case. Look at the interaction term of your factorial model: that says it all in this case. The heterogeneous slopes test has an effect size Z less than 1 (0.68) which means the angular difference is not exciting relative to the reduced model (test of homogeneous slopes).

 

Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

https://faculty.sites.iastate.edu/dcadams/

Hi Dean,

Thank you very much for the explanation and response! Yes, I both "fit_size <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) * groups" for allometry, and "fit_TA <- procD.lm(coords~groups*stages, data = gdf_size)" for trajectory analysis both yields Z < 1, with the latter yields Z<0. They did confirm the very insignificant group allometry and trajectories.

However, as you can see, when submitting these linear models to homogeneity of slopes test & trajectory analysis, the Z value both >1 (1.5 and 1.4 respectively), though the p-values appear to be marginally insignificant:

Group allometry vectors:

> PW3 <- pairwise(fit_size, groups = as.factor(gdf_size$groups), covariate = log(gdf_size$Csize))
> summary(PW3, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC",
   angle.type = "deg")
Result:
                        r                      angle             UCL (95%)        Z                   Pr > angle
control:test   0.6477955    49.6244          51.05174        1.506624      0.077
Group trajectories:
>TA <- trajectory.analysis(fit_TA,  groups = gdf_size$groups,  traj.pts = gdf_size$stages, print.progress = FALSE)

> summary(TA, attribute = "TC", angle.type = "deg") 

Pairwise correlations between trajectories, plus statistics
                        r                   angle          UCL (95%)      Z                   Pr > angle
control:test  0.5863598   54.10089  57.12142       1.475715      0.083

If I did not read the help file and associated papers wrong, the group allometry vectors and trajectories are both calculated based on the fitted values of the full linear models (fit)size and fit_TA respectively). Should the results of Z be more consistent with correspondent ProcD.lm?  On the other hand, though I did not post previously, the Z-values for comparing vector lengths did show Z <0 and Z = 0.455. Those are very small values, perhaps the insignificant interaction factor is more associated with vector length nor angles.

I do agree that 2D plot can be tricky for high-dimensional space. However, for the 2D PC1-PC2 plot of trajectory analysis in particular, it appears that PC1 and PC2 account for more than 90% of the total variance of the fitted values to the linear model. Should this graph weigh a bit more in reflecting two trajectories are more or less parallel in the multidimensional space?

Thanks again for your time!

Chi

Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Differences in size-shape plotting & ANOVA vs homogeneity of slopes test, so did the trajectory analysis

 

Dear all,

 

I am testing the differences in allometry in a test and control group of mice. Each group has two ontogenetic stages: P28 and P60.

 

1) I ran an ANOVA to test interaction between size & groups first. The results shows an insignificant interaction effect (p-value = 0.258).

 

> fit_size <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) * groups,  data = gdf_size,
print.progress = FALSE)

 

                                 Df        SS                 MS              Rsq           F               Z              Pr(>F)    
log(Csize)                1   0.024298    0.0242978    0.35307     9.8733     4.2532      0.001 ***
groups                     1   0.011943     0.0119432    0.17355     4.8531     3.6215      0.001 ***
log(Csize):groups  1   0.003046     0.0030464    0.04427     1.2379     0.6874      0.258    
Residuals                 1. 2 0.029532  0.0024610    0.42912                        
Total                          1. 5 0.068819   

 

The regScore & Predline plotting also confirm the very similar allometric trajectories in two groups by running (output plot attached):

> plotAllometry(fit_size, size = gdf_size$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "RegScore",
pch = 19, col = as.numeric(interaction(gdf_size$groups)))

> plotAllometry(fit_size, size = gdf_size$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "PredLine",
pch = 19, col = as.numeric(interaction(gdf_size$groups)))

 

2) However, the test of homogeneity of slopes using 'Pairwise()' shows a large angle of 49 degree between the allometric slopes of two groups, though the p-value 0.077. 

 

> PW3 <- pairwise(fit_size, groups = as.factor(gdf_size$groups), covariate = log(gdf_size$Csize))
> summary(PW3, confidence = 0.95, test.type = "VC",
   angle.type = "deg")

Result:

                        r                      angle             UCL (95%)        Z                   Pr > angle
control:test   0.6477955    49.6244          51.05174        1.506624      0.077

 

Even though the result shows insignificance, but an angle of 49 degree appears to be too large as the RegScore and PredLine plots showed nearly parallel allometric trajectories.

 

I hope I can directly use 'fit_size', which is 'coords~log(Csize)*Groups'. I assume it would randomize the size*group interaction to test the differences between  size-shape slopes in each group

 

I then did an additional trajectory analysis since each group has two distinct ontogenetic stages: P28 and P60. Therefore, the linear model includes an interaction of group*stage:

 

>fit_TA <- procD.lm(coords~groups*stages, data = gdf_size)

 

You can also see that 'fit_TA' shows an insignificant effect of "group*stage" interaction (p-value = 0.550):

>summary(fit_TA)

                          Df       SS           MS                Rsq           F               Z               Pr(>F)    
groups              1    0.018256   0.0182560   0.26528   5.6613    3.05408     0.001 ***
stages               1   0.009202    0.0092017   0.13371   2.8535    2.46277     0.025 *  
groups:stages  1   0.002665    0.0026647   0.03872  0.8264    -0.13343     0.550    
Residuals          12  0.038696   0.0032247   0.56229                          
Total                 15   0.068819   


>TA <- trajectory.analysis(fit_TA,  groups = gdf_size$groups,  traj.pts = gdf_size$stages, print.progress = FALSE)

>TP <- plot(TA,  pch = as.numeric(as.factor(gdf_size$groups)) + 20, bg = as.numeric(as.factor(gdf_size$stages)),  cex = 0.7,  col = "gray")

>add.trajectories(TP, traj.pch = c(21, 22), start.bg = 1, end.bg = 2)

 

You can see the attached plot of trajectories showed nearly parallel lines, consistent with Procrustes ANOVA and allometry plotting. 

 

However, again, the test of angles between two trajectory vectors showed a large angle of 54.1 degree, though the p-value is 0.083.

 

> summary(TA, attribute = "TC", angle.type = "deg") 

 

Pairwise correlations between trajectories, plus statistics
                        r                   angle          UCL (95%)      Z                   Pr > angle
control:test  0.5863598   54.10089  57.12142       1.475715      0.083

 

Could you give me some advice about this sharp differences between angles calculated from test of slopes vs. plotting & ANOVA? Did I construct the linear model run for test of slopes & trajectory angles? Thank you very much!

 

Chi

Chi,

 

Human intuition fails us on interpreting angles in high-dimensionsal spaces. One cannot interpret an angle of say, 45 degrees and consider it large or small based on what we think in a 2D space.

 

In high-dimensional spaces there are many, many directions that confer such an angle, which may explain why it is not surprising (ie not significant) in your case. Look at the interaction term of your factorial model: that says it all in this case. parts:
Dear Chi,

Optics can be deceiving with geographic variables, which is why Z scores are more reliable.  For example, consider the following graph:


In a trajectory analysis, the angle between solid vectors would be larger than the angle betted dotted vectors, but the former would have a smaller Z score (most likely) than the latter, because all vector points are rather clumped.  Assuming somewhat equal scatter of points around these mean values, the large angle for the solid vectors is probably not significant if there is a lot of scatter around the points.  An angle is calculated based on least squares estimates of mean values, but one would question if it should be calculated, as a more parsimonious conclusion is that the vectors do not mean much compared to one point in the middle of these points.  By contrast, even with moderate scatter around the points for the dotted vectors, the comparatively smaller angle is probably significant with a large Z score.  It would be silly to expect a single point in the middle as a good way to model phenotypic change.  Regardless of whether certain vectors significantly diverge, if V1 is a principal component, it explains much variation.  (The components are calculated based on fitted values, not the orientation of trajectories.

It seems like your result point to conditions like the solid lines, not like the dotted lines.

Best,
Mike

Even though the result shows insignificance, but an angle of 49 degree appears to be too large as the RegScore and PredLine plots showed nearly parallel allometric trajectories.

 

I hope I can directly use 'fit_size', which is 'coords~log(Csize)*Groups'. I assume it would randomize the size*group interaction to test the differences between  size-shape slopes in each group

>summary(fit_TA)

stages               1   0.009202    0.0092017   0.13371   2.8535    2.46277     0.025 *  
groups:stages  1   0.002665    0.0026647   0.03872  0.8264    -0.13343     0.550    
Residuals          12  0.038696   0.0032247   0.56229                          
Total                 15   0.068819

>TP <- plot(TA,  pch = as.numeric(as.factor(gdf_size$groups)) + 20, bg = as.numeric(as.factor(gdf_size$stages)),  cex = 0.7,  col = "gray")

>add.trajectories(TP, traj.pch = c(21, 22), start.bg = 1, end.bg = 2)

 

You can see the attached plot of trajectories showed nearly parallel lines, consistent with Procrustes ANOVA and allometry plotting. 

 

However, again, the test of angles between two trajectory vectors showed a large angle of 54.1 degree, though the p-value is 0.083.

 

> summary(TA, attribute = "TC", angle.type = "deg") 

 

Pairwise correlations between trajectories, plus statistics
                        r                   angle          UCL (95%)      Z                   Pr > angle
control:test  0.5863598   54.10089  57.12142       1.475715      0.083

 

Could you give me some advice about this sharp differences between angles calculated from test of slopes vs. plotting & ANOVA? Did I construct the linear model run for test of slopes & trajectory angles? Thank you very much!

 

Chi

On Sat, Aug 3, 2024 at 5:05 AM Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dear Chi,

Optics can be deceiving with geographic variables, which is why Z scores are more reliable.  For example, consider the following graph:


In a trajectory analysis, the angle between solid vectors would be larger than the angle betted dotted vectors, but the former would have a smaller Z score (most likely) than the latter, because all vector points are rather clumped.  Assuming somewhat equal scatter of points around these mean values, the large angle for the solid vectors is probably not significant if there is a lot of scatter around the points.  An angle is calculated based on least squares estimates of mean values, but one would question if it should be calculated, as a more parsimonious conclusion is that the vectors do not mean much compared to one point in the middle of these points.  By contrast, even with moderate scatter around the points for the dotted vectors, the comparatively smaller angle is probably significant with a large Z score.  It would be silly to expect a single point in the middle as a good way to model phenotypic change.  Regardless of whether certain vectors significantly diverge, if V1 is a principal component, it explains much variation.  (The components are calculated based on fitted values, not the orientation of trajectories.

It seems like your result point to conditions like the solid lines, not like the dotted lines.

Best,
Mike

Group allometry vectors:

Pairwise correlations between trajectories, plus statistics

control:test  0.5863598   54.10089  57.12142       1.475715      0.083

 

If I did not read the help file and associated papers wrong, the group allometry vectors and trajectories are both calculated based on the fitted values of the full linear models (fit)size and fit_TA respectively). Should the results of Z be more consistent with correspondent ProcD.lm?  On the other hand, though I did not post previously, the Z-values for comparing vector lengths did show Z <0 and Z = 0.455. I do agree that 2D plot can be tricky for high-dimensional space. Should this graph weigh a bit more in reflecting two trajectories are more or less parallel in the multidimensional space?

 

Thanks again for your time!

 

Chi

 

 

On Tue, Jul 30, 2024 at 6:44 AM 'Adams, Dean [EEOB]' via geomorph R package <geomorph-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

Chi,

 

Human intuition fails us on interpreting angles in high-dimensionsal spaces. One cannot interpret an angle of say, 45 degrees and consider it large or small based on what we think in a 2D space.

 

In high-dimensional spaces there are many, many directions that confer such an angle, which may explain why it is not surprising (ie not significant) in your case. Look at the interaction term of your factorial model: that says it all in this case. The heterogeneous slopes test has an effect size Z less than 1 (0.68) which means the angular difference is not exciting relative to the reduced model (test of homogeneous slopes).

 

Dean
